at_a_glance.state_note: Practice and gallery activity are documented; institutional and auction evidence are sparse.
at_a_glance.title: At a glance
at_a_glance.summary: Marc Chalmé is a French figurative painter whose constructed interiors, quiet streets, landscapes, still lifes, and occasional figures are organized around controlled light and suspended time. Recent documented works are mainly oil on canvas, with drawings and oil on board also present. His career record is primarily commercial-gallery based, with solo presentations in Paris, New York, Boston, London, Zurich, and St. Moritz. No public-museum collection record was verified, and accessible public-auction coverage consists of one price-restricted 2021 record, preventing meaningful price statistics or trend analysis.

biography_and_career.state_note: Schools, degrees, teaching post, current base, and the venue of the reported 2005 first solo exhibition are not specified.
biography_and_career.title: Biography and career development
biography_and_career.summary: Artist and gallery biographies state that Chalmé studied in Nantes and Rennes, later studied with Georges Pichon, and has divided his time between painting and teaching since 1991. The published career chronology is structured around commercial galleries in France, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland.

artistic_practice.state_note: Supported by documented works, two gallery accounts, and one independent specialist review; no artist-authored statement was located.
artistic_practice.title: Artistic practice
artistic_practice.summary: Chalmé repeatedly uses legible, carefully constructed architecture, objects, and landscapes while minimizing narrative action. Dusk, night, artificial illumination, windows, reflections, empty rooms, and partly deserted streets recur. An independent review identifies the construction of interior and exterior space and the interaction of shadow and light as central. Galleries extend this reading toward dream, temporal suspension, and the uncanny. The synthesis that light functions as the primary event is system-generated, not an artist statement.
